meta.titre: Simple machines: levers, ramps and efficiency

sections.contenu_markdown: A farmer in the Menoua division lifts a heavy stone out of a field with a long iron bar, and a trader pushes a barrow of tomatoes up a plank into a lorry. Neither of them changes the amount of work needed; they use simple machines that let a small force do a job that would otherwise need a big force. The GCE O/L paper asks you to name types of lever, to find the mechanical advantage, velocity ratio and efficiency of a machine, and to explain why a long handle helps.

items: Work done equals force times distance moved in the direction of the force, $W = Fd$.
The moment of a force about a pivot is the force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed; in a real machine some energy is wasted as heat by friction.

sections.titre: Simple machines: MA, VR, efficiency and levers
sections.contenu_markdown:
A **simple machine** is a device that makes work easier by changing the size or the direction of a force. Levers, inclined planes, wheel and axle, pulleys and screws are all simple machines. Three ratios describe any machine:

- **Mechanical advantage:** $\text{MA} = \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}$ (no unit).
- **Velocity ratio:** $\text{VR} = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by the effort}}{\text{distance moved by the load}}$ (no unit).
- **Efficiency:** $\eta = \dfrac{\text{MA}}{\text{VR}} \times 100\% = \dfrac{\text{work output}}{\text{work input}} \times 100\%$.

In an ideal machine $\text{MA} = \text{VR}$ and $\eta = 100\%$. In a real machine friction makes $\text{MA} < \text{VR}$, so $\eta < 100\%$. No machine gives more work out than is put in; it only trades a smaller effort for a larger distance.

**Levers** turn about a pivot (fulcrum). In an ideal lever the principle of moments gives $\text{effort} \times \text{effort arm} = \text{load} \times \text{load arm}$, so $\text{VR} = \dfrac{\text{effort arm}}{\text{load arm}}$. The arms are measured from the pivot.

| Class | Position | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| First | pivot between the effort and the load | see-saw, scissors, crowbar, pliers |
| Second | load between the pivot and the effort | wheelbarrow, bottle opener, nutcracker |
| Third | effort between the pivot and the load | tweezers, fishing rod, forearm |

A longer effort arm gives a larger VR, so a smaller effort lifts the same load. A hydraulic jack is also a force-multiplying machine, with VR equal to the ratio of the piston areas in the ideal case.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a load is pushed or pulled up a ramp or slope.
variantes.contenu_markdown: The effort moves along the slope while the load rises vertically: $\text{VR} = \dfrac{\text{length of slope}}{\text{vertical height}}$. A longer, gentler slope has a higher VR, so a smaller effort is needed, but the load has to be moved over a greater distance. Friction between the load and the slope reduces the efficiency.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a large wheel turns a small axle, such as a windlass, a screwdriver handle or a steering wheel.
variantes.contenu_markdown: $\text{VR} = \dfrac{\text{radius of the wheel}}{\text{radius of the axle}}$. The effort is applied at the rim of the wheel and the load is attached to a rope around the axle. When the load rises a distance $h$, the effort at the rim moves $\text{VR} \times h$.

sections.enonce_markdown: A farmer uses a crowbar to lift a stone of weight $900\ \mathrm{N}$. The crowbar has an effort arm of $1.2\ \mathrm{m}$ and a load arm of $0.20\ \mathrm{m}$. The farmer needs an effort of $180\ \mathrm{N}$, and when the stone rises $0.050\ \mathrm{m}$ his hands move $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$. Calculate (a) the velocity ratio, (b) the mechanical advantage, (c) the efficiency.

etapes.action: Calculate the velocity ratio from the distances.
etapes.justification: VR is the effort distance divided by the load distance.

etapes.action: Check VR with the lever arms.
etapes.justification: For a lever, VR is also effort arm divided by load arm, and the two must agree.
MA is load divided by effort.
Efficiency is MA divided by VR, as a percentage.
Work input is effort times effort distance and work output is load times load distance.

sections.conclusion_markdown: VR = **6**, MA = **5** and the efficiency is **83.3 %** (the missing energy is wasted by friction at the pivot).

items.erreur_markdown: A student calculates the velocity ratio of a lever by dividing the load by the effort.
items.pourquoi_faux: Load divided by effort is the mechanical advantage. The velocity ratio uses distances (or arm lengths), not forces.

items.erreur_markdown: A student obtains an efficiency of 125 % and states that the machine is very good.
items.pourquoi_faux: An efficiency above 100 % would mean more work out than in, which is impossible. MA and VR have been swapped.

items.erreur_markdown: A student measures the effort arm of a lever from the load instead of from the pivot.
items.pourquoi_faux: Both arms are perpendicular distances from the pivot.
items.correction_markdown: Measure effort arm and load arm each from the pivot.

items.erreur_markdown: A student classifies a wheelbarrow as a first-class lever.
items.pourquoi_faux: In a wheelbarrow the pivot is the wheel axle at one end, the load is in the middle and the effort at the handles: the load is between the pivot and the effort, a second-class lever.
items.correction_markdown: Locate the pivot, the load and the effort, then compare their positions.

items.erreur_markdown: A student claims that a machine with VR = 5 gives five times more work.
items.pourquoi_faux: The effort is smaller, but its distance is larger. Work output is never greater than work input.
items.correction_markdown: Say the machine multiplies the force (up to five times in the ideal case) but not the work.

items.enonce_markdown: A plank $5.0\ \mathrm{m}$ long is used as a ramp to raise a drum of weight $1000\ \mathrm{N}$ onto a platform $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$ high. An effort of $250\ \mathrm{N}$ along the slope is needed. Calculate the velocity ratio, the mechanical advantage and the efficiency.
items.solution_markdown:
$\text{VR} = \dfrac{\text{length of slope}}{\text{height}} = \dfrac{5.0}{1.0} = 5$.

$\text{MA} = \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}} = \dfrac{1000}{250} = 4$.

$\eta = \dfrac{\text{MA}}{\text{VR}} \times 100 = \dfrac{4}{5} \times 100 = 80\%$.

**VR = 5, MA = 4, efficiency = 80 %.** (Check with work: input $250 \times 5.0 = 1250\ \mathrm{J}$, output $1000 \times 1.0 = 1000\ \mathrm{J}$, so $\tfrac{1000}{1250} = 80\%$.)

items.enonce_markdown: A wheel and axle has a wheel of radius $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ and an axle of radius $0.050\ \mathrm{m}$. An effort of $100\ \mathrm{N}$ at the rim of the wheel lifts a load of $480\ \mathrm{N}$ hung from the axle. Calculate (a) the velocity ratio, (b) the mechanical advantage, (c) the efficiency, and (d) the length of rope pulled at the rim of the wheel when the load rises $0.50\ \mathrm{m}$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\text{VR} = \dfrac{R}{r} = \dfrac{0.30}{0.050} = 6$.

(b) $\text{MA} = \dfrac{480}{100} = 4.8$.

(c) $\eta = \dfrac{4.8}{6} \times 100 = 80\%$.

(d) Effort distance $= \text{VR} \times \text{load distance} = 6 \times 0.50 = 3.0\ \mathrm{m}$.

**VR = 6, MA = 4.8, efficiency = 80 %, rope pulled = 3.0 m.**

items.enonce_markdown: A wheelbarrow carries a load of $600\ \mathrm{N}$ whose line of action is $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$ from the axle of the wheel. The handles are held $1.2\ \mathrm{m}$ from the axle. (a) To which class of lever does the wheelbarrow belong? (b) What is the effort needed in an ideal case? (c) In practice an effort of $250\ \mathrm{N}$ is needed. Calculate the MA and the efficiency. (d) By how much must the hands rise to lift the load $0.050\ \mathrm{m}$?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The pivot (wheel axle) is at one end, the load is between pivot and hands. It is a **second-class lever**.

(b) $\text{VR} = \dfrac{\text{effort arm}}{\text{load arm}} = \dfrac{1.2}{0.40} = 3$. In the ideal case $\text{effort} = \dfrac{600}{3} = 200\ \mathrm{N}$. **Ideal effort = 200 N.**

(c) $\text{MA} = \dfrac{600}{250} = 2.4$ and $\eta = \dfrac{2.4}{3} \times 100 = 80\%$. **MA = 2.4, efficiency = 80 %.**

(d) Effort distance $= \text{VR} \times 0.050 = 0.15\ \mathrm{m}$. **The hands rise 0.15 m (15 cm).**

items_markdown: $\text{MA} = \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}$, $\text{VR} = \dfrac{d_E}{d_L}$ and $\eta = \dfrac{\text{MA}}{\text{VR}} \times 100\%$; efficiency is always below $100\%$ in a real machine.
For a lever, $\text{VR} = \dfrac{\text{effort arm}}{\text{load arm}}$, with both arms measured from the pivot.
First-class: pivot in the middle. Second-class: load in the middle (wheelbarrow). Third-class: effort in the middle (tweezers).
Inclined plane: $\text{VR} = \dfrac{\text{length of slope}}{\text{height}}$. Wheel and axle: $\text{VR} = \dfrac{R}{r}$.
Machines multiply force at the cost of distance; they never give more work than the work put in.
